Marking the Boat to Find the Sword: Why Does an Accurate Mark Still Lead Us Astray?
A man from the state of Chu was crossing a river by boat when his sword fell into the water.
He immediately cut a mark into the side of the boat and said:
“This is where my sword fell.”
The boat continued on its way.
When it reached the bank, he jumped into the water beside the mark to look for the sword.
The sword had not traveled with the boat.
So, of course, he could not find it.
This fable is often used to mock someone who cannot adapt.
The world has changed, yet he clings to his old method.
But if we say only “Don't be rigid,” we easily overlook the part of the story most worth questioning:
**There was nothing wrong with the mark.**
The sword really had fallen from that spot.
The problem was not an inaccurate record, but the kind of relationship the record preserved.
At the moment the sword fell, the mark and the point where it entered the water occupied the same position.
If the boat had stayed still from then on, diving beside the mark might indeed have led to the sword.
But once the boat began moving, the mark remained faithfully on that plank. What it accurately preserved was:
The sword fell beside this part of the boat.
What it did not preserve was:
The sword is still beside this plank now.
Those two statements coincided at the moment of the fall, then parted company.
The man from Chu remembered a genuine fact but forgot that the relationship on which it depended had changed.
His problem, then, was not a lack of memory.
Quite the contrary: he was so faithful to the mark memory had left that he stopped checking whether the mark and its object were still connected in the same way.
We need markers.
Without them, it is hard to preserve the past or allow people at different times to draw on the same experience.
Maps, rules, names, records, assessments, and promises all do something similar: they fix an important relationship at a particular moment, so that we do not have to begin from scratch each time.
The problem is that what has been fixed stays unchanged more easily than the world does.
An assessment may have been written long ago, and the person may since have acquired new abilities. Yet the assessment still arrives ahead of them in every new setting.
A rule may have been established to address a certain risk. The risk's source and distribution have changed, but the rule continues to operate in its original form.
Someone may also carve a mark into themselves on the basis of the past:
“I'm no good at this.”
“This is how I always am in relationships.”
“That failure proves this path isn't for me.”
All these judgments may have had a factual basis when they formed.
But they preserve relationships under a past set of conditions, not necessarily positions valid at every later moment.
A marker is not necessarily wrong just because it is old.
What we really need to ask is:
Has the object it marks moved?
And has the thing carrying the marker moved?
Immediately after telling the story, the Lüshi Chunqiu applies it to law and government.
When times have moved on but laws have not adjusted to the relevant conditions, it is like diving beside an old mark on a boat that has already traveled on, hoping to find the sword.
This context makes the fable more demanding than a general call to “be flexible.”
It does not say that all old rules should be discarded.

If the relationship a rule addresses still exists, stability is precisely its value. People need to know that promises will not change for the sake of a little convenience, and that shared standards will not shift with the mood of the powerful.
Change cannot therefore become an excuse to abolish every rule.
A person cannot merely say “Things are different now” and cease to honor a promise. Nor can an institution declare its old procedures obsolete whenever they become inconvenient.
The key is not age, but relevance.
Which condition made the original rule reasonable?
Does that condition still exist?
Has an irrelevant detail changed, or has the position through which the rule locates its object shifted?
The boat's movement matters because the mark is on the boat while the sword remains in the water. Had the sword been tied to the boat, its movement would not have invalidated the mark.
Not every change is relevant.
Knowing which change alters the relationship is what it really means to “examine the present.”
This also explains why simply demanding that we “keep up with the times” is not enough.
Someone can constantly change their methods, vocabulary, and appearance without ever understanding the problem anew.
If the man from Chu cut a fresh mark every time the boat traveled a little farther, he would get no closer to the sword. He would merely be updating the wrong reference point more often.
Change itself is not the answer.
What must change is how we understand the marker.

The mark belongs to the boat; the sword belongs to the place where it fell. To find the sword, we need a reference that remains connected to its position in the water, rather than more information worked into a moving boat.
Likewise, updating a rule does not mean changing its date or making its language fashionable.
It requires us to explain anew:
What was this rule meant to protect?
Whose actions have changed?
Who now bears a different share of the risk?
What should remain stable, and what would betray the rule's original reason if it did not change?
Without answers to these questions, “innovation” and “conservatism” may both amount to more marks on the boat.
There is also something sympathetic about the man from Chu.
When the sword fell, it happened quickly.
He needed to do something at once. Making a mark at least gave him a feeling that he had not completely lost control.
We often do something similar when confronted with change.
We first seize on something we can preserve: an explanation, a label, a procedure. These give the disorder a temporary boundary.
That need not be a mistake.
The mistake often comes later.
The danger has passed, but we never look back to check whether the marker used in an emergency still fits today's object.
A provisional judgment can become a permanent identity.
A management method that worked in a crisis can continue to claim every decision after the crisis ends.
A boundary once established to protect a relationship can, years later, remain only as a wall that keeps everyone out.
Past markers have reasons of their own.
Respecting those reasons does not mean obeying their positions forever.
The story is easily understood as a conflict between memory and reality.
In fact, it reveals something more precise:
A memory can be entirely true and still be insufficient to guide present action.
Because a fact is never merely an isolated point.
It also contains relationships between an object and its surroundings, an action and its conditions, a marker and its reference.
Preserve only one end, and once the relationship changes, even accuracy can produce a wrong result.
Being responsible to the past does not mean carrying every form it left behind into the present unchanged.
Real responsibility means knowing why something was done then, and remaining willing, when conditions change, to preserve that reason rather than only its shell.
In the end, the man from Chu jumps into the water beside the mark.
His action is perfectly consistent with his record.
He has neither forgotten nor betrayed the original plan.
Yet the sword is still not there.
This is the fable's sternest point:
Faithfully following a rule that has lost touch with its object will not restore that object, however faithful the execution.
The greatest danger may not be an old mark.
It may be a mark that has forgotten what it is marking.

*Textual basis: the passage beginning “A man of Chu was crossing a river” in the Lüshi Chunqiu, “Examinations on Taking Great Care,” “Examining the Present.” After the story, the original explicitly states that “the boat has moved, but the sword has not,” comparing this to laws left unchanged after the times have moved on. This essay distinguishes the accuracy of a marker itself, the relationship it preserves, and its applicability after that relationship changes.*
